analysis.one_liner: Makes it an unfair labor practice for employers to permanently replace striking workers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 189 cosponsors—180 of 257 House Democrats and 9 of 175 House Republicans—but never got a committee vote, dying in the House Education and Labor Committee when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under longstanding labor law, employers may permanently replace workers who go on strike. This bill would make that illegal: an employer could not offer anyone permanent-replacement status for doing a striker's job during a labor dispute, and could not give any hiring preference to someone who worked, or said they were willing to work, over a striker who exercised union rights and was still willing to work. It would have been enforced the same way other unfair labor practices are, through the National Labor Relations Board.
analysis.who_benefits: Striking workers and their unions. A striker could no longer lose their job permanently for exercising the right to strike; the employer would have to take them back once the dispute ended.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to grant or offer 'permanent replacement employee' status to anyone doing bargaining-unit work during a labor dispute.

Bars an employer from giving any hiring or employment preference to someone who worked, or was willing to work, during a dispute over an employee who exercised union rights and remains willing to work for the employer.
Protects strikers by adding this prohibition to Section 8(a) of the National Labor Relations Act, the list of employer unfair labor practices enforceable by the National Labor Relations Board.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with unionized workforces, who would lose the ability to permanently replace striking workers—a tool that gives employers leverage in long strikes and keeps a business running without committing to hiring strikebreakers permanently.

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove an employer's ability to grant permanent replacement status during a labor dispute, meaning a company hit by a strike could no longer make binding, permanent hires to fill struck jobs; it could keep operating with temporary arrangements only.

Critics of striker-replacement bans argue that the current rule—affirmed in a 1938 Supreme Court decision allowing permanent replacements—gives both sides an incentive to settle strikes quickly, and that removing it would shift bargaining power heavily toward unions and could make strikes longer or more common. That trade-off is inherent in the bill's design; it deliberately reweights that balance toward workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For striking workers, the benefit is direct and large: the strike becomes a real, survivable option rather than a gamble with the job itself. The cost falls on employers, who lose a powerful bargaining tool and would have to manage strikes with temporary labor only. Honest supporters would acknowledge that the change makes strikes easier to call and potentially harder to settle from the employer's side; that is the point of the bill, and the question is whether the bargaining balance should tilt that way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 1990, sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to its Labor-Management Relations Subcommittee, which held a hearing in June 1990—but no committee vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. William (Bill) Clay of Missouri introduced H.R. 3936 in the House on February 1, 1990.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction.
On February 28, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations.
On June 6, 1990, executive comment was requested from the Department of Labor.
The subcommittee held hearings on June 13, 1990; that was the furthest the bill progressed.
The bill ended the session with 189 cosponsors—180 of 257 House Democrats and 9 of 175 House Republicans—and never received a vote in the committee or on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead: with the bill dead, they kept the legal right to permanently replace striking workers, and striking workers kept bearing that risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who kept the striker-replacement right

for.name: Rep. William (Bill) Clay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 1, 1990 and gathered additional sponsors.

for.name: 189 House cosponsors (180 of 257 House Democrats, 9 of 175 House Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill broad majority-level support in the House.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 1, 1990 and never brought it to a committee vote; it was sent to the Labor-Management Relations Subcommittee, which held one hearing in June 1990 and no markup followed.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed striker-replacement bans, arguing employers need the ability to keep operations running during strikes; the broader striker-replacement fight drew sustained employer lobbying in this period.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic—180 of 257 House Democrats—though 9 of 175 House Republicans also cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote that would have shown the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would strip employers of the power to permanently replace striking workers, their main leverage in long strikes. Workers would keep their jobs after a strike instead of risking permanent loss of them.
Unions would gain a much stronger strike weapon: members could strike without risking their permanent jobs. The union interest runs alongside strikers' own interest here.
